https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp8.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Martin Ryan was convicted of spying earlier this year - charges both he and France denied By Paul Kirby Europe digital editor Published 1 hour ago French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying. His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov. Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev. However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe. It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list. Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns. Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years. Usmanov was cited by the EU in its 2022 listing , external as having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine". The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans". Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men. Foreign Minister Baiba BraÅ¾e said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive". Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative". French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations. Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon. Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government. Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China. "I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court. Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Mamedli was not among the 20 prisoners pardoned by Aliyev. The demonstrations had been largely peaceful during the day. But serious disturbances erupted in the evening in several places. Frankfurt witnessed some of the worst scenes, with rioters smashing shop windows and looting stores, while police reported attacks with Molotov cocktails Image: Kai Pfaffenbach/REUTERS Rioters smashed shop windows with street signs and other objects, and set rubbish bins on fire Image: Boris Roessler/dpa/picture alliance Special police units were deployed as unrest continued late into the night. Police reported around 30 people taken in custody in Frankfurt. Image: Andreas Arnold/dpa/picture alliance In Cologne, around 200 people, some of them rioters, were involved in disturbances around the city's cathedral, directly next to the main railway station Image: Christoph Reichwein/dpa/picture alliance After repeated clashes in Cologne, police dispersed a large crowd outside the cathedral to de-escalate the situation Image: Thomas Banneyer/dpa/picture alliance The demonstrations in Germany are inspired by similar movements in France and Italy calling for political elites to heed the concerns of the younger generation Image: Florian Wiegand/dpa/picture alliance In Berlin, police broke up a demonstration after officers were attacked with stones and protesters set off fireworks. According to police, 27 officers suffered minor injuries and up to 56 protesters were temporarily detained Image: Ralf Hirschberger/AFP Edited by: Roshni Majumdar https://p.dw.com/p/5Oupz Skip next section Clashes break out in Cologne, five detained 11/01/2026 November 1, 2026 Clashes break out in Cologne, five detained Akanksha Saxena with dpa Police officers were pelted with bottles and bicycles outside the cathedral Image: Thomas Banneyer/dpa/picture alliance Clashes broke out in Cologne on Saturday, with about 200 people involved in disturbances near Cologne Cathedral. Police officers were attacked on the square outside the famous cathedral, with bottles and bicycles hurled toward them. One person was injured, police said. Authorities detained five people. In a nearby side street, a window was smashed by an electric scooter thrown during the unrest, police said. A smashed window at an art gallery in central Cologne Image: Christoph Reichwein/dpa/picture alliance According to regional broadcaster WDR, other groups besides Gen Z demonstrators were involved in riots. Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was deeply saddening that peaceful protests were overshadowed by "extremists who had nothing but violence in mind." While Gen Z protests across Germany were largely peaceful during the day, clashes were reported in several cities as night fell. Edited by: Roshni Majumdar https://p.dw.com/p/5Ouoy Skip next section Frankfurt police seal off major shopping street after rioting and looting 10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 Frankfurt police seal off major shopping street after rioting and looting Akanksha Saxena People looted goods from stores in Frankfurt Image: Andreas Arnold/dpa/picture alliance German police sealed off a major shopping street in central Frankfurt on Saturday night after rioters smashed shop windows, looted stores and attacked officers following a demonstration. Police closed Die Zeil, one of Germany's busiest shopping streets, to incoming visitors and urged bystanders to leave the area. "Anyone not involved who is still on the Zeil can leave. Access to the Zeil is no longer possible," Frankfurt police said in a post on X and in loudspeaker announcements. Chaotic scenes unfolded along the shopping street, where dpa journalists witnessed people breaking into stores and stealing trainers and other goods. A specialist firearms shop was also targeted, prompting several arrests, a police spokesman said. Police also reported attacks on officers, including attacks involving incendiary devices. A fire burns in the street in Frankfurt Image: Kai Pfaffenbach/REUTERS The violence erupted after police broke up a demonstration organized as part of the nationwide "Gen Z regelt" (roughly meaning "Gen Z takes charge") protests. A large contingent of officers was deployed around the Zeil, with authorities advising people to avoid the area or leave central Frankfurt. Edited by: Kieran Burke https://p.dw.com/p/5Oufi Skip next section Gen Z protests 'very peaceful,' says police union official 10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 Gen Z protests 'very peaceful,' says police union official After a day of youth protests in Germany, senior police union representative Andreas Rosskopf said that there was no widespread property damage "so far." "The Gen Z protests have turned out to be very peaceful," Rosskopf told the daily Rhenische Post . While confrontations were reported after the marches ended in multiple cities, the people driving the clashes were "individuals acting independently, some of whom were masked." Rosskopf, who represents Germany's federal police , said security forces acted very decisively and forcefully when such response was appropriate. "Security forces remain absolutely ready to prevent any further clashes in the late evening of overnight," he said. Edited by: Kieran Burke https://p.dw.com/p/5Ouf4 Skip next section Minor scuffles reported as German protests wrap up 10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 Minor scuffles reported as German protests wrap up German security forces reported minor violent incidents in several cites in the wake of the Gen Z demonstrations. In Hamburg , protesters at the city's Steintor square pelted the police with fireworks . Police used "immediate force" to clear the area, including using a water cannon. Several police officers were injured during a similar incident in Frankfurt, according to a state interior minister. Police also used a water cannon in Cologne , where the march was halted and turned into a stationary rally after some protesters covered their faces and used pyrotechnics. A police officers sustained light injuries in nearby Bonn during a confrontation with a group of protesters. In Berlin , the authorities noted a rally separate from the official event organized by the Gen Z movement. Police initially reported "isolated instances of throwing eggs and bottles" from a crowd of around 500 people. The authorities later also reported "illegal burning of pyrotechnics" and said the crowd has grown to around 3,000 participants. "One officers could be injured more seriously, but this will need some more looking into," said Hesse Interior Minister Roman Poseck. "We assume there were about 100 attackers motivated by extreme leftist ideology," the state minister said. "They have staged a massive attack against the police by throwing bottles, stones and fireworks." Police responded with water cannons and have the situation in hand, he said Edited by: Kieran Burke https://p.dw.com/p/5OuZI Skip next section IN PICTURES: Germany's Gen Z take to the streets 10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 IN PICTURES: Germany's Gen Z take to the streets Most of the protests in Germany ended peacefully despite high tensions Image: Ina Fassbender/AFP Thousands of young people took part in protests in 34 German cities on Saturday. The protests in Germany were inspired by similar events in France Image: Uli Deck/dpa/picture alliance German Gen Z protesters called out rising living expenses, remilitarization of Germany, and declining education. Many young people in Germany are angry over the state funneling money into military spending rather than education or the social safety net Image: Jonas Walzberg/REUTERS Some of the protesters also called for Germany's current chancellor, center-right Friedrich Merz, to step down. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is facing political pressure and low approval levels Image: Pia Bayer/dpa/picture alliance The protests were held under the slogan Gen Z regelt (Gen Z sorts it). Businesses in various parts of Germany barricaded their stores to protect them from looting Image: Michael Probst/AP Photo/picture alliance Police were out in force after many politicians warned that Germany will not tolerate the kind of violence seen in France in mid-October. The authorities warned they would not tolerate violence against first responders Image: Ralf Hirschberger/AFP Police reported incidents in which pepper spray and water cannon were used to keep crowds under control, with protesters setting off fireworks and lighting fires. Some protesters in Hamburg set construction barriers on fire Image: Marius Bulling/onw-images/dpa/picture alliance Most of the demonstrations ended peacefully. While no nationwide turnout estimate was immediately available, the police faced smaller crowds than previously anticipated Image: Focke Strangmann/dpa/picture alliance But tensions remained high in some German cities with reports of several police officers injured. Germany's Berlin is considered a stronghold of left-leaning political groups Image: Christian Mang/REUTERS Edited by: Kieran Burke https://p.dw.com/p/5OuVx Skip next section Hamburg: Protesters set fire to barriers 10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 Hamburg: Protesters set fire to barriers Police said they used a water cannon to extinguish the fire Image: Marius Bulling/onw-images/dpa/picture alliance In Germany's second-biggest city, Hamburg, police estimated 6,700 people taking part in the demonstration. They reported some groups of black-clad protesters, some of whom also wore face masks, pulling apart construction site barriers and throwing them on the street. Some of the barriers were later set on fire. Police said they pushed the crowd back and used pepper spray to break them apart. The fire was eventually put out. The organizers, "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z sorts it) gave a much higher number, saying 10,000 people were in attendance. One of the speakers in Berlin, Kaja Schwab, decried false promises made by politicians. The youth is being told that "we will do well if we work hard enough." In reality, the life is getting unaffordable and the young are "forced into military service," she said, in reference to Germany's renewed recruitment drive . Early police estimates included: Berlin: Around 650 people gathered at the historic Brandenburg Gate Frankfurt: More than 1,500 attended a rally near the European Central Bank. Munich: Around 1,000 people attending the march Mainz: Police counted around 1,200 participants, situation "peaceful" Freiburg: Around 2,500 people attended, according to police. Hundreds also gathered in Hamburg, Erfurt, Magdeburg, Dresden, Leipzig, Nuremberg, and elsehwere. No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available. More than 182,100 people had expressed interest in attending the events online.
